q: What is command-query separation?
short: Meyer's principle: every method should either perform an action (command, changes state) or return data (query), but not both.
example: pop() violates it; split into peek() and remove().

q: What is CQRS?
short: An architectural pattern separating command handling (writes) from query handling (reads), often with separate write and read stores synchronised via projections/events.
detail: Reduces contention, simplifies permissions, scales reads.
example: Write store of trips vs read store of trip summaries.

q: What is eventual consistency?
short: In a distributed system an update may not be visible everywhere immediately, but all replicas converge to the same state after synchronisation.

q: How does RAG work?
short: Ingest documents (chunk, embed, index in a vector store); at query time embed the question, retrieve the most similar chunks, insert them into the prompt and generate a grounded answer.

q: Why is RAG described as pipe-and-filter plus CQRS?
short: Ingestion and querying are each chains of filters (pipe-and-filter), and they are separated into a write path (ingestion into the vector store) and a read path (retrieval and generation), i.e. CQRS.

q: What does a vector store do?
short: Stores embeddings with IDs, text and metadata and answers similarity queries (nearest neighbours) quickly using indexes such as HNSW.

q: Monolith vs microservices?
short: Monolith: one deployable unit, shared memory, simple to test/deploy, but whole-app scaling, tech lock-in, growing complexity. Microservices: independent single-responsibility services, independent scaling/deployment/tech, at the cost of network calls and operational complexity.

q: What is the monolithic ML pattern?
short: UI/API, model loading, preprocessing and prediction logic in one codebase and deployment unit, good for prototypes, simple, low latency, but hard to scale independently and redeployed for every model update.
example: Notebook model wrapped in one API.

q: State the single-responsibility principle.
short: Gather together the things that change for the same reasons; separate those that change for different reasons (Robert C. Martin).
follow: How does it apply to classes?

q: Describe a microservices ML demo layout.
short: API gateway/prediction service routes requests; model service loads the model and only infers; logging service stores requests and predictions; each scales independently.
mistakes: Synchronous logging on the critical path.

q: What problems does CQRS solve on the data side?
short: Data contention when reads and writes hit the same rows in parallel (shared/exclusive locks), complex security because every entity is both read and written, and mismatched shapes for read-optimised vs write-optimised models.

q: Implement a minimal event-sourced CQRS flow.
short: CommandSide.handle() appends immutable events to a log and stream; a projector consumes events to update a read model; queries read only the read model. Show lag before projection completes.

q: Your RAG assistant answers confidently with wrong policy details. Diagnose.
short: Check retrieval (are the right chunks retrieved? chunk size, embeddings, stale index), prompt (instruct to use context only and cite), generation (model ignoring context), and evaluation (faithfulness, context precision/recall).

q: RAG vs fine-tuning?
short: RAG supplies knowledge at query time (fresh, citable, cheap to update); fine-tuning changes model weights (style, format, domain behaviour) but is costly to update and doesn't cite. Often combined.
example: Policies via RAG; tone via fine-tuning.
mistakes: Fine-tuning to add frequently changing facts.

q: How do you choose a chunk size?
short: Balance: small chunks lose context, large chunks add irrelevant text and token cost. Chunk on semantic boundaries (headings, paragraphs), add overlap, keep metadata, and tune using retrieval metrics on a labelled question set.

q: Contextual vs non-contextual embeddings?
short: Non-contextual (GloVe) give one vector per word regardless of context; contextual (BERT, Sentence-BERT) depend on surrounding text and work better for semantic search.

q: When would you move a monolithic model service to microservices?
short: When prediction load needs independent scaling (e.g. GPU), when release cadences differ (model weekly, UI daily), when teams own different parts, or when failures in one part must not take down others.

q: What does an API gateway do in a microservices system?
short: Single entry point that routes requests to services, handles cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, TLS, aggregation), and hides internal service structure from clients.
mistakes: Putting business logic in the gateway.

q: How do you handle read-your-own-writes in a CQRS system?
short: Return the new state or a version token from the command, route the user's next reads to the write store or wait until the projection reaches that version, or show optimistic UI with a 'syncing' state.
example: Data scientist registers model and immediately lists versions.

q: Design a RAG system for 10 million documents updated hourly.
short: Incremental ingestion via change events; chunking with metadata and access-control tags; batch embedding service; sharded vector store with HNSW; hybrid search (BM25 + vectors) and re-ranking; caching; per-document versioning; evaluation and monitoring of retrieval quality and freshness.

q: What is approximate nearest-neighbour search and its trade-off?
short: Indexes like HNSW, IVF or PQ find most true nearest neighbours while comparing far fewer vectors; trade a small recall loss for large speed/memory gains, tuned with parameters (e.g. ef, M).
follow: How do you measure ANN recall?

q: What new problems do microservices introduce for ML systems?
short: Network latency and serialisation, distributed tracing/debugging, version compatibility between feature and model services, data consistency across services, deployment orchestration, and more infrastructure cost.
detail: Mitigate with contracts, tracing, service mesh.
example: Feature service schema change breaks model service.

q: Where does eventual consistency hurt in ML systems?
short: Training-serving skew when features in the online store lag the offline store, inconsistent model versions across replicas affecting A/B tests, and dashboards lagging incidents. Mitigate with versioned features, sticky routing and lag monitoring.
example: User sees different recommendations per request.

q: Your company wants every service to be a microservice from day one for a new ML product. Respond.
short: Recommend a modular monolith first with clear internal boundaries (SRP), automated tests and CI/CD; extract services when scaling, team or release needs justify it; keep the model behind an interface so it can move to its own service later.
example: Start with one FastAPI app with separate modules.
